title: You May be Able to Get 43 More Minutes of Work Done if You Change Your Desk - Nautilus
content:
Have you ever wished you had an extra hour in the day? Well, if you’ll settle for roughly 45 minutes, I’ve got good news for you. A new study published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics found that workers can squeeze 43 minutes of extra productivity out of their day, just by using a sit-stand desk. 

A team of occupational and public health researchers from Texas A&M University discovered the productivity benefits of these adjustable-height desks, which exploded in popularity around the time sitting was declared “the new smoking,” after studying more than 10,000 workers who worked at a large California energy company. They surveyed the workers about their comfort and tracked their computer activity digitally, capturing everything from keystrokes and mouse clicks to words typed and typos.

Read more: “Your Boss Is Watching You”

They found that workers who used the height-adjustable desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time per day, compared with just 2.95 hours among those using old-fashioned sit-only desks. Over a year, that adds up to roughly 170 hours of work or four 40-hour workweeks. The sit-standers also made more keystrokes and typed more words (although this speedy typing resulted in slightly more typos). Both groups were equally comfortable (or uncomfortable).  

The productivity gains could add up to big bucks, too. According to their back-of-the-envelope calculations using a $52 per hour wage, sit-stand desks may be able to generate roughly $9,000 in annual productivity value per employee (this is where your boss’s eyes turn into dollar signs). 

“Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” study author Mark Benden said in a statement. “The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way.”

There’s one caveat, however: This wasn’t a randomized controlled trial. Instead of being randomly assigned workstations, employees were allowed to choose whether they wanted a sitting or standing desk as part of a company wellness program. It’s possible that the more conscientious workers simply opted for adjustable desks. 

Still, there are countless studies on the health risks posed by living a sedentary life, so if you don’t want a height-adjustable desk for your productivity, consider one for your health.

title: Joe Biden’s New Memoir Shows a Man in Denial
author: @NewYorker
content:
The last time Joe Biden published a memoir, called “Promise Me, Dad,” nine years ago, he ended up getting his ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, in a certain amount of trouble. Zwonitzer had recorded interviews he conducted with Biden, including one in February, 2017, at Biden’s rental home in Virginia, in which the then former Vice-President told him, “I just found all the classified stuff downstairs!” That recording would eventually become public because more classified stuff would later be found at a University of Pennsylvania office that Biden used, and then still more at his Delaware home, leading to the appointment of a special counsel, Robert Hur, in 2023. Zwonitzer was subpoenaed, had his computer taken, faced the prospect of criminal charges, and was referred by House Republicans for contempt of Congress. Years of litigation ensued.

Zwonitzer, who also worked with Biden on a 2007 memoir, “Promises to Keep,” is not mentioned in the former President’s latest offering, “Promise Me, America,” which is out next week. (Judging from the acknowledgments, Biden relied on a number of people this time, among them Ted Widmer, a historian whose recent work includes a volume on the Declaration of Independence and an oral history of the band Wings.) Biden gives an account of the classified-documents investigation that focusses, instead, on his rage at Hur, who wrote, in his final report on the case, that the President came across, in his interview with the special counsel, as a “sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory.” Biden calls this “extraneous commentary” and a “gratuitous hit.” It was neither. Biden’s forgetfulness was a reason that Hur cited for not prosecuting the President: if a jury believed that Biden had honestly forgotten about the classified documents, it would have been hard to get a conviction.

By any reckoning, the question of Biden’s general competency during his Presidency is a crucial one; doubts about his fitness ended his campaign for reëlection, after all. But “Promise Me, America” treats all such inquiries as extraneous and gratuitous, not just Hur’s. Biden allows that his June, 2024, debate with Donald Trump (who had his own issues with classified documents) had “gone badly” but adds that “debates had gone badly for lots of incumbent Presidents.” He sees no qualitative distinction between his frightening and heartbreaking lack of focus that night and Barack Obama’s subpar performance against Mitt Romney, or George W. Bush being “caught with a scowling face” in his debate with John Kerry: “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate.” Biden continues to find it unfair that he was not afforded that opportunity. He blames “the narrative” and disloyal Democrats for the fact that he had to drop out, which he did three and a half weeks after the debate. “I wasn’t living in a dream world,” he writes. “I believed I was the best person to lead the world.”

Incredibly, Biden sticks to that position, even though, in May, 2025, when his second term would have barely been under way, he announced that he had been diagnosed with Stage IV prostate cancer. The disease had metastasized to his bones and, based on what is known as its Gleason score of nine, was fast-moving. His doctors, it emerged, had stuck to the general practice of not routinely screening men older than seventy. (Biden turned eighty in 2022.) In his memoir, Biden answers the question of whether this was wise when the patient was the Commander-in-Chief with a resounding “maybe.” He adds that he was surprised that people were “cynical” enough to think that he might not have been honest about his health. (In February, 2024, three weeks after the Hur report, that same medical team declared him “healthy, active, robust” and “fit for duty.”) It took an interview with People magazine this week to wrest from him the concession that, had he known he had advanced cancer, he wouldn’t have run. “But that wasn’t the case,” he said, still insisting that on “an objective basis” he was the right man for the job. The People interview has been his only one tied to the release of the memoir; in an X post, he said that there wouldn’t be a traditional press tour because the cancer treatment sometimes “slows me down.”

The news of the memoir, in short, is that there is no real news: Biden is as stubbornly in denial as ever. And that assessment risks making the book sound more interesting than it is. Apart from the few, frustrating stretches on his reëlection decision (from which one would never know that he had once referred to himself as “a bridge,” a phrase widely understood to mean that he would serve only a single term), most of “Promise Me, America” is startlingly dull. Much of it has the feel of something written by a committee—and a committee of which Biden himself need not have been a member. Even the headline-making detail, from an early excerpt, in The Atlantic, that on entering the White House in January, 2021, Biden found a note from Trump that was more friendly and circumspect than one would expect from a man who had been trying to overturn the election—“I know how much you love the American people”—is of marginal interest, and really about Trump, not Biden. The advance Biden received for the book was reportedly about ten million dollars.

There are whole pages that read as if someone simply sat down with Biden’s public schedule and speeches and patched them together with a few judicious additions of the first person (“As I said in my welcoming remarks . . .”) and references to America’s past (Lincoln, the gold rush, D Day). A description of a meeting in the Situation Room includes the names and job titles of a dozen people, followed by nothing much illuminating about how they may have interacted or clashed, or about how power in the White House actually worked. Some attendance lists are compelling in themselves, such as the log of phone calls that Biden made in the hours after he dropped out. (Bill Clinton is on it; Obama is not.) But when intimate details about encounters with senators or world leaders do appear, they too often have footnotes that lead to contemporary press coverage or public statements. The source listed for Angela Merkel’s blunt criticism of Trump, for example, is a Guardian article about her memoir. Instead of any real introspection, we get cliché. After a mention of threats posed by China and Russia: “Given these choppy waters, I was glad to be steering the ship of state.”

One of the themes of Biden’s memoir is that he was a fantastic President. To hear him tell it, as his term was coming to an end, things were going great all around. The global economy was “humming,” inflation in the U.S. was falling, we’d “completely rebuilt NATO” and “reclaimed the American advantage over China,” carbon emissions were poised to plunge, and the A.I. companies had meekly fallen in line with his call for them to be more responsible actors. And there were real successes. It would be a far better book if he acknowledged some failure other than not retaining the loyalty of Democratic leaders.

For example, as part of his claim to have beaten COVID, he writes that it took him just four months, until May, 2021, to go “from fewer than half of America’s schools being open to 99 percent.” If that number is news to many parents, it is because Biden seems to be defining “open” as a school where a child showed up at some point, rather than consistently or full time, and ignoring reclosures in the wake of the Omicron variant. (An earlier book, Franklin Foer’s “The Last Politician,” explored the role Joe Biden’s relationship with teachers’ unions played in the struggle to reopen schools, for better or worse.)

There is similar sleight of hand in his discussion of immigration. Biden boasts of a dramatic fall in “encounters with undocumented migrants” at the border between January, 2021, and January, 2025. At the same time, the Biden years did see a historic wave of immigration, and the memoir offers little insight into how it was managed. For example, he does not mention his Administration’s concurrent extension or renewal of Temporary Protected Status to more than a million people, and of humanitarian parole to hundreds of thousands more, many of whom were fleeing terrible circumstances. Those migrants were documented, but, because T.P.S. grants and parole are executive-branch actions, Biden also left them vulnerable to having their status stripped away by the next Administration—which it promptly began doing, as Trump turned migrants into targets.

“Yes, people could point to moments when I mixed up names or lost my train of thought or had a weak voice or walked slowly,” Biden writes. “But they could never point to something presidential that I failed to do.” A few pages later, he points to one. It is the spring of 2024, several months after Hamas brutally murdered civilians in Israel, including at a music festival, taking many of the survivors hostage, and Biden has repeatedly spoken to Benjamin Netanyahu to express his “concerns” about the Israeli military response, and what “rising casualties were doing to Israel’s image.” To his dismay, he writes, “Bibi had no qualms about making promises he had no power—or intention—to keep.” Be that as it may, it also appears that the promises Netanyahu made—to act with restraint, to protect civilians—were ones that Biden no longer had the strength or resolve to enforce. The combination of an ever-mendacious Netanyahu and an increasingly diminished Biden was a disastrous one. In many situations, a good team of staff members can act on behalf of a President, but there are moments when a President is required to impose his or her will, as only a President can. That moment came for Biden after October 7th, and he missed it.

Biden’s wife, Jill Biden, published her own memoir earlier this year. To read them side by side is to be reminded that there is more than one way of being avoidant. Jill padded her book with details about the White House’s floral arrangements; Joe does so with a six-page list of laws he signed, including the CHIPS and Science Act and the Working Dog Health and Welfare Act. The Biden Administration did accomplish a great deal—the legislation passed, the trillions of dollars spent—but it could be notably lacking in transparency, and the President’s memoir doesn’t much help. He speaks more kindly of his Vice-President, Kamala Harris, than Jill does, for example, but without giving a real sense of her influence or why he thought that she would be ready to step in for him, either when he chose her as his running mate or when he endorsed her, twenty-seven minutes after he withdrew from the race.

Where the Jill and Joe memoirs converge is in their repeated, deeply felt invocations of Biden’s older son, Beau, who died of brain cancer in 2015. (Both Bidens also view the younger, troubled Biden son, Hunter, as a martyr-like target of partisan attacks; neither expresses regret for Joe’s decision to grant him, along with other relatives and allies, a broad pardon before leaving office.) Beau’s appearances are the most Bidenesque part of “Promise Me, America,” and the places where Biden’s own mark is most clear. The promise in “Promise Me, Dad,” the 2017 memoir, was Beau’s request that Joe not be so undone by his death that he withdrew from politics.

Beau is also part of Biden’s explanation for his enduring anger at Robert Hur, who said in his report that Biden didn’t know what year it was that Beau died. In his memoir, Biden calls this claim “outrageous,” adding, “if Robert Hur wants to know when my son died, here’s my answer: Today. I wake up every day feeling like I just lost him a minute ago.” But the transcript of their interview shows that Hur was correct. The Hur report matters because, in retrospect, it offered Democrats an opening to replace Biden on the ticket, at a time when only four states had held primaries, and Super Tuesday was still a month away, making it less likely that a decent President would be replaced by an awful one. But it matters in assessing Biden’s memoir, too.

Throughout his career, Biden’s signature rhetorical subject has been how a person pushes on in the face of grief and mourning. As a young man, he lost his first wife and his baby daughter in a car crash. He had it in him to write a great book about the loss of his own powers as he aged, and how it led him to lash out at people like Hur, who said what they saw, and at allies who loved him but knew that he was done. He might have found a way to be grateful for a debate that, aberration or not, insured that he wouldn’t take the oath of office with an undiagnosed case of cancer, and regretful that he didn’t depart the stage even sooner. That this memoir is not that book is a literary as well as a political tragedy. The one thing Biden doesn’t know how to mourn, it seems, is his Presidency. ♦

title: Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum
author: Amy Howe
content:
The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to decide whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket, which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

The Department of Homeland Security issued guidance that (among other things) barred any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The guidance also indicated that anyone who entered the country despite Trump’s suspension of entry would be quickly removed without some of the procedural protections provided by law.

The challengers in the case are a group of 13 individuals who say that they have been persecuted or tortured in their home countries, as well as three immigration-related nonprofits. They sought to file a class-action lawsuit in federal court in Washington, arguing that both the proclamation and the guidance violate federal immigration law.

U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss recognized a class of challengers, made up of immigrants who are or would be subject to Trump’s proclamation. He concluded that the DHS guidance was unlawful and threw it out, and he barred DHS officials from implementing those actions under the proclamation.

A three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit initially paused part of Moss’ order, but a different panel later largely upheld it on the merits. Judge J. Michelle Childs, joined by Judge Cornelia Pillard, wrote that the “text, structure, and history” of federal immigration law “make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts. The Proclamation and Guidance are thus unlawful to the extent that they circumvent … removal procedures and cast aside federal laws affording individuals the right to apply and be considered for asylum or withholding of removal protections,” a more limited form of protection from deportation.

Judge Justin Walker dissented in part. Although he contended that Trump has the discretion to deny all asylum applications and therefore can dispense with the application process altogether on the ground that he would deny the applications, he agreed with the majority that the government “cannot remove aliens to countries where they will be persecuted, and the Proclamation and Guidance cannot strip them of mandatory procedures that protect against that removal.”

The D.C. Circuit agreed to keep its ruling on hold while the government appeals, allowing the government to maintain the asylum restrictions.

Contending that the U.S.-Mexico border “had become overwhelmed by an ungovernable influx of millions of aliens, creating chaotic conditions that criminal and terrorist organizations exploited to threaten our national security,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that “suspending the illegal entry of aliens and precluding their access to asylum” is “[t]he most important and effective pieces of the President’s response.”

Trump’s proclamation, Sauer continued, “rests on a commonsense understanding of the President’s inherent and delegated powers to exclude aliens.” Therefore, he said, Trump “acted well within his authority in preemptively indicating that asylum applications filed by aliens who violate the proclamation’s entry suspension would be denied—and in effectuating that discretionary policy choice by directing that the government need not accept futile asylum applications from those aliens.”

Sauer also told the court that the lower courts did not have the power to apply their order to a whole class of challengers. Federal immigration law, he argued, expressly bars lower courts from issuing orders that require federal officials to enforce or implement specified provisions of federal immigration law –including those “allowing aliens to assert an asylum claim … and obtain a hearing before being subject to expedited removal.”

And in any event, Sauer continued, the class of challengers also violates the rules governing class actions because it “sweeps in aliens who are currently overseas and have no imminent plans to enter the United States (much less enter illegally).” Those noncitizens, he wrote, have not been injured and therefore cannot be part of the class; they “will become future class members here only if they choose to illegally enter the county.”

The challengers urged the justices to deny review, telling them that the D.C. Circuit’s ruling “correctly held that the President may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.” They also pushed back against the administration’s suggestion that the proclamation and guidance were intended to address an “unprecedented crisis,” countering that “the facts say otherwise. By January 2025, before the Proclamation took effect, border apprehensions had returned to historically routine levels, down over 90 percent from their peak. If the Executive Branch nonetheless believes it needs new tools to manage the border, Congress must provide them.”

The statute on which Trump relies for the proclamation, the challengers continued, “does not speak to the removal of noncitizens who are already here. Nor does it authorize the Executive Branch to abrogate Congress’s protections against removing noncitizens to persecution or torture.” Instead, they wrote, federal immigration law “provides that noncitizens ‘may apply’ for asylum, ‘irrespective of … status’” or where and how they entered the United States. In conflict with “statutory command,” the challengers contended, “the Proclamation and Guidance dictate that statutorily eligible noncitizens may not apply for or receive asylum.”

The challengers also rejected the administration’s suggestion that the lower courts could not have broadly barred the Trump administration from implementing the proclamation and guidance. The law stripping the lower courts of the power “to enjoin or restrain the operation of” some federal immigration laws does not apply here, they said, because Trump’s proclamation relies on other laws that are not implicated by that bar.

The court agreed to consider the legality of Trump’s proclamation and the guidance, as well as Moss’ power to enter an order providing broad relief, but it turned down the government’s request to weigh in on whether the class violates the rules governing class actions.

The court also agreed to hear Robinhood Markets v. Sodha on Friday, involving whether a California-based financial-services company violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering in July 2021, although that data was not scheduled to be reported until August of that year. In a lawsuit brought by investors, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit ruled against the company, prompting it to come to the Supreme Court in February.

The company asked the justices to decide two questions, involving the effect of the company’s failure to disclose interim financial data that investors may consider significant to their decisions on compliance with federal securities laws and regulations.

The investors asked the justices to stay out of the case, telling them that “[t]here is nothing radical … about the decision below,” much less anything worthy of the Supreme Court’s intervention. Although the company “disagree[s] with the outcome,” the investors said, it “do[es] not propose that this Court adopt legal rules in place of the existing standards.”

In a brief filed last month at the court’s request, the Trump administration agreed with Robinhood that the court should weigh in on the first question presented by the company’s petition for review. Sauer told the justices that the 9th Circuit’s ruling “threatens significant untoward consequences.”

The court on Friday agreed to decide one of the questions posed by Robinhood Markets’ petition: “[w]hether an issuer can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong” of the law at the center of the dispute “based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of” that provision, “without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.”

The justices will likely hear oral arguments in these cases sometime next spring.

Recommended Citation: Amy Howe, Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 13, 2026, 3:44 PM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/supreme-court-agrees-to-hear-case-on-trump-administrations-suspension-of-asylum/

title: Apex Legends adds a grumpy, teamwiping Godzilla to its growing history of unappealing crossovers
author: James Archer
content:
Bad breath

No doubt eager as peas to help pay off EA's billions in debt, battle royale shooter Apex Legends is set to run another of its intellectual propertytastic crossover events. This one, starting on November 10th, stars Godzilla, of Godzilla Minus Zero, Godzilla vs. Kong, Godzilla (1954), Godzilla 2000: Millennium, Godzilla (1998), Son of Godzilla, and Godzilla (2014). I might be missing some.

Besides a profitable range of weapon and character skins, most of which appear to have hot glue gunned an 70-year film franchise's worth of dorsal fins all over themselves, the King of the Monsters himself will show up on the game's Storm Point map. He does at least have more than a background cameo: he'll occasionally blast an area with Legend-melting atomic breath, though brave souls who risk the danger zone can score a custom Devotion LMG with a unique heat ray attack of its own.

Worth noting also that the character skins are each based on a certain 'zilla movie, though as our freelance news writer and associate Large Lizard Cinema expert Ashley isn't working today, I'm not sure which of these are from hits and which are the duds. Walking wallhack motherfucker Bloodhound gets the newest fashion, their skin being inspired by Minus Zero, while my personal favourite Scottish scientist Horizon gets duds based on Big G in Godzilla vs. Destoroyah. Octane's skin is taken from... something called a Jet Jaguar? Google suggests this may in fact be elite Godzilla knowledge, something I clearly lack.

Regardless, and with the understanding that a lot of effort goes into these crossovers, I still kinda wish they didn't exist? Even putting aside basic game-playing problems with how, for example, wacky skins interfere with Legend silhouettes – you couldn't pay me to initiate a fight against a full team of near-identical Gundampeople - it's just icky to have an otherwise sharp, smart, at times fiercely competitive battle royale turned into an animated billboard for a few days.

Besides, Apex already has its own kaiju: the sleepy, pacifist Leviathans that innocently wandered into the King's Canyon map for a few of the earlier seasons. I consider these much better Friend Material than Godzilla, on the grounds that they'd only kill you by accident, and it was usually your own fault - by wandering under their briefly raised megahooves - anyway.

title: As Arc Raiders celebrates its first birthday, publisher Nexon reveals the extraction shooter has topped 17 million sales, but revenue is set to decline
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Embarking up the right tree.

Arc Raiders, Embark Studios' popular extraction shooter, has exceeded 17m copies sold, according to publisher Nexon.

Arc Raiders was released at the end of October 2025, so reaching that milestone in a year is nothing to scoff at. According to Nexon's latest earnings report, however, only 1m copies of those 17 were sold in the third quarter - meaning sales have certainly slowed down.

Relatedly, Nexon said it expects Arc Raiders' revenue to decline in the fourth quarter compared to the same period last year - when the game enjoyed its hugely successful launch - and anticipates revenue will be "broadly flat sequentially". Despite this, the company said Arc Raiders' revenue was "within the outlook", naming its Frozen Trail update as a key moment that brought back some lapsed players while introducing new ones.

Indeed, Frozen Trail boosted the game's Steam player count, and reports suggest it also helped Arc Raiders hit a six-month player high across various platforms.

Even with its slowing sales, Arc Raiders remains one of Nexon's most successful titles. The company primarily attributed an overall year-on-year revenue increase, for the nine months ended 30th September, to the game.

Looking ahead, the biggest question hanging over Arc Raiders is whether or not it's going to get a dedicated PvE playlist. Following a successful test earlier this summer, Embark has been coy, and hasn't said whether PvE will return as a permanent feature. Arc Raiders' Chinese version does have a dedicated PvE mode, and executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said he could see both PvP and PvE modes co-existing in the future.

title: Nintendo game sales surge thanks to Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, but Switch 2 hardware suffers big decline
author: Sherif Saed
content:
Yenning for more.

Nintendo's latest financial earnings report is here, revealing healthy software sales thanks to the enormously popular Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. Sales of Switch 2 hardware, however, are down.

As per Nintendo's 2nd Quarter fiscal earnings report, focusing on the three-month period ending 30th September 2026, Switch 2 hardware registered a big drop in sales during the first half of the current financial year (FY27).

Over that period, Nintendo sold 6.49m Switch 2 units and 1.27m units of the original Switch - equating to a 37.4 percent decline for Switch 2 and 32.7 percent decline for Switch 1 compared to the same period last year. Nintendo had previously forecast a decline in hardware sales, and the company still expects to sell 16.50m Switch 2 units by the end of the current fiscal year.

Nintendo software sales, on the other hand, saw a big year-on-year boost of 18.8 percent on Switch 2 (to 24.49m units) and a smaller increase of 6.8 percent on Switch 1. That's all thanks to the release of several popular first- and third-party titles over the first half of FY27. Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream was by far the most successful game with 8.81m units sold, followed by Rhythm Heaven Groove at 2.89m. Splatoon Raiders (the only Switch 2 exclusive of the three) sold 2.42m. Nintendo also highlighted a 60.5 percent year-on-year increase in digital game sales.

The increase in software unit sales and the "continued weakness of the Yen" couldn't prevent the overall business from declining by 15.3 percent year-on-year, however.

Other remaining releases in Nintendo' s current fiscal year include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (which launches today and was awarded five stars in Eurogamer's review), Switch 2 re-releases of Pikmin 2 and Xenoblade Chronicles 3, as well as Metroid Ravenous, which arrives early in 2027.

title: Switch 2 and Switch consoles updated to version 23.5.0 as Nintendo quietly re-introduces eShop gifting
author: Dom Peppiatt
content:
Bow out.

Nintendo has just pushed out a new update to all Switch and Switch 2 consoles, bringing the firmware on both up to version 23.5.0. The headline change with the new update is support and compatibility for an upcoming update that will allow members of a Nintendo Account family group to gift games to one another.

The feature itself is expected to go live on 17th November, 2026. "Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," says a post on a dedicated blog on the Nintendo site. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs. As a reminder, anyone with a Nintendo Account can easily set up a family group and add members (up to 8 total)."

The publisher notes, however, that "some products may not be eligible for digital gifting" and that "supervised accounts are not able to send digital gifts". Additionally, "the number of digital gift purchases allowed in a given period is limited".

"This feature is a great way to celebrate a special occasion with your kids. Happy gifting!" concludes Nintendo. Just in time for the holidays, how thoughtful. It's worth noting that a previous iteration of this support was included back on the Nintendo Wii, but that was much more robust than this - back then, the publisher allowed users to send WiiWare or Virtual Console games to anyone on their Wii Friend list via the Wii Shop Channel, rather than just those limited to their immediate group. This functionality was lost in 2019, alongside the closure of the Wii Shop Channel.

The patch also came with some other updates, you can see those listed below.

  • Added the ability to configure accessibility settings during first-time setup.
  • Information on these accessibility settings can be found in Nintendo Switch 2 first-time setup.
  • Added support for an upcoming feature to allow gifting of Nintendo eShop products to a Nintendo Account family group member.
  • This gifting feature will be available after a Nintendo eShop update, scheduled for November 17, 2026.
  • The following updates have been made in Accessibility in System Settings:
  • Added Portuguese (Portugal) to “Text to Speech” languages.
  • Added Portuguese (Portugal) to the GameChat “Convert Text to Speech” languages.
  • General adjustments and fixes were made to improve the user experience

title: Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature
author: James Archer
content:
Have you played...?

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

title: Wardogs is hitting 185,000 accounts with a ban wave as Season 3 lands
author: Vikki Blake
content:
Ruff justice.

Wardogs' Season 3 will launch on 12th November, complete with a new urban map, a new Limited Mode, and a ban wave targeting 185,000 accounts.

Developer Bulkhead confirmed the details earlier this week, revealing plans for a full wipe and progression changes that it hopes will "recapture the shared discovery and sense of achievement that defined" the 100-player tactical shooter when it first launched in Early Access.

The new map will focus on close-quarters fighting, and for a "more level playing field", players can dip into Limited Mode, which offers "an alternative way to experience" the game as it restricts weapons, ammunition, armour, and vehicles.

While the full list of restrictions is still being decided, it currently includes FMJ-only ammunition, a Tier 2 armour cap, and a reduced attack vehicle selection.

"The mode is designed to preserve the feel of early-to-mid-game combat and reduce the advantage offered by more powerful equipment," the team said.

Bulkhead also confirmed seasons are getting longer. From now on, they’ll last three months, giving players "more time to work towards their goals before each wipe and the development team more time to prepare future updates". Progression will also be "brought closer to the pace of Season 1", following the studio’s acknowledgement that Season 2 accelerated "the journey too aggressively".

"Season 3 is about giving players a new battlefield to learn together and a progression journey worth spending time on," said Bulkhead CEO Joe Brammer. "Longer seasons give everyone more room to reach their own goals, and give us the time to properly develop what comes next."

Alongside Season 3, Bulkhead revealed it has used machine learning to review is "activating further layers of its anti-cheat" after analysing 187 million hours of gameplay with help from machine learning. It says having close to four million unique players since launch gave it enough data to pull that work forward from next year.

"[E]xploiters, real-money traders, and gold-farming networks" have been permanently banned and lost their server-hosting privileges, and a player trust score is planned for 2027.

"Protecting the people who play Wardogs fairly is essential to everything we're building," Brammer added.

Bigger changes to the metagame, including a new progression system, are also due in 2027 as Bulkhead works towards Wardogs 1.0. Full Season 3 patch notes will be out before launch.

Wardogs launched in Steam Early Access on 10th September, and is due on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2028.

Wardogs is one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

title: AMD has patched its SSD-eating GPU driver bug with an optional Adrenalin update for RX 7000-series graphics cards and above
author: Andy Edser
content:
I reported earlier this week on a bug within AMD's GPU driver suite, wherein a misfiring utility was accused of making huge amounts of erroneous storage writes. Some AMD graphics card owners reported their SSD health dropping by up to 1% per month, but a fix has finally arrived.

AMD Adrenalin Edition 26.11.1 is an optional update, which means you'll need to download the installer yourself. However, according to the topline notes, the update fixes "excessive writes to the system drive" at idle for Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards and above.

AMD's wording suggests that older GPUs might not be affected by the bug, but some of the user reports mention RX 6000-series cards, so it's unclear if a fix for earlier models is still in the works.

I also think it's a slightly odd move to make this an "optional" update, given the severity of some of the reports, though this is often how AMD deals with getting fixes out in between official driver releases—by the looks of the known issues, this interim driver might still need some work before it's patched into the next full release.

AMD lists a litany of potential issues with various games, including crashes and driver timeouts in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, War Thunder, and Cyberpunk 2077 with FSR enabled. These issues, however, match and are fewer than in the previous driver release, with the exception of the Phantom Blade Zero bug.

The company notes that "visual corruption may appear on character hair while playing Phantom Blade Zero on Radeon RX 9000 series graphics products." I'm currently working my way through PBZ myself, and the idea of turning down the quality settings on Soul's magnificent hairdo? Sacrilege, as far as I'm concerned.

Still, I'd definitely consider downloading the update if my SSD health was rapidly being eaten by a misfiring utility. Buying a replacement these days isn't cheap, so anything that prevents unnecessary wear and tear on existing hardware is a-okay with me.
